title: Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2016
short_title: Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2016

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would cut the portability period for age pension and some other payments from 26 weeks to six weeks for holidays overseas.
It would also end two student support payments and freeze income test thresholds for working-age allowances and student payments for three years.
The changes would start on 1 January 2017, or later if the act receives royal assent after 1 October 2016, with specific start dates for each measure.
changes: Reduce the time overseas pensioners can receive full basic rate from 26 weeks to six weeks.
Abolish the pensioner education supplement and the education entry payment.
Freeze the income free areas for working-age allowances (except student payments) and for single parenting payment for three years.
Freeze the income free areas, other means test thresholds, and student income bank limits for student payments for three years.
summary.affected: Age pension recipients, a small number of other payment recipients with unlimited portability, pensioner education supplement and education entry payment recipients, and people receiving working-age allowances (including student payments).

speeches.speaker: Christian Porter
speeches.brief: Moved to discharge four government bills from the Notice Paper: the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures) Bill 2016, the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2016, the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Youth Employment) Bill 2016, and the Fairer Paid Parental Leave Bill 2016.

speeches.speaker: Tony Burke
speeches.brief: A Labor MP supported discharging four social services bills—the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures), Budget Repair, Youth Employment, and Fairer Paid Parental Leave bills—but criticised the government for refusing to explain the decision. He argued the government still backed the measures and would reintroduce them, noting it had conceded that $13.5 billion of its claimed $16 billion fiscal gap with Labor would not pass parliament.
